fundamentals.title: How the browser builds a page
fundamentals.outcome: Trace how source files become a rendered, interactive page and use browser tools to inspect it.

lessons.title: The web platform
lessons.focus: HTML describes structure, CSS presentation, JavaScript behavior, and the browser provides runtime services.

objectives: Explain what HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and browser APIs each contribute.
Trace a user action from markup to a visible response.
explanation: A browser is both a document renderer and a runtime. HTML describes meaningful content and controls; CSS determines their presentation; JavaScript responds to events and updates the document. Browser APIs expose capabilities such as storage, networking, timers, and accessibility-related state.

These layers cooperate through standard interfaces. The browser parses HTML into a DOM tree, applies CSS rules, and exposes DOM elements to JavaScript. A button's behavior should start with a real button element, which already supports keyboard activation and focus, rather than a styled generic container.

walkthrough: HTML provides a keyboard-operable control and a status region.
JavaScript subscribes to the button's click event, then changes text content.
The browser updates the rendered page and announces the status change to assistive technology.

misconceptions: JavaScript does not replace semantic HTML; using the correct element gives users built-in behavior.
A browser API is not the same as an external library. APIs are capabilities provided by the browser runtime.

check.prompt: A clickable <div> looks like a button but cannot be activated with the keyboard by default. Which layer should you fix first, and why?
check.answer: Use a <button> element first. HTML semantics provide keyboard activation and focus behavior; CSS can style it, and JavaScript can add the action.
check.explanation: Starting with the semantic control reduces custom code and gives assistive technologies a correct role.

lessons.title: DOM, CSSOM, and rendering
lessons.focus: Relate source markup and styles to the document tree, style rules, layout, paint, and interaction.

objectives: Describe the DOM and CSSOM as browser representations of source files.
Put parsing, style calculation, layout, paint, and compositing in a useful order.
explanation: The HTML parser creates the DOM (Document Object Model), a tree of elements and text. The CSS parser creates the CSSOM (CSS Object Model), a representation of applicable style rules. The browser matches rules to elements and computes styles, then calculates geometry (layout), draws pixels (paint), and combines layers (compositing).

This sequence is a useful model, not a promise that every update repeats every stage. Changing an element's width usually affects layout and later stages. Changing opacity can often be handled later in the pipeline. Browser optimizations vary, so measure before assuming a property is cheap.

example.code:
Studio hours

Open weekdays, 9:00–17:00.
walkthrough: The parser creates main, h1, and p nodes in the DOM.
A matching .notice rule contributes declarations to computed style.
The browser lays out the text and box, paints visible pixels, then composites layers for display.

misconceptions: The DOM is not the original HTML string; it is a live object model built from parsed markup.
A repaint and a relayout are different costs. A visual change does not always require recalculating geometry.

check.prompt: You change a card's background color without changing its size or position. Which pipeline work is generally needed, and which stage may be avoided?
check.answer: The browser must update the card's painted appearance. It may avoid recalculating layout because geometry did not change; exact optimizations depend on the browser.
check.explanation: This tests the pipeline model while allowing for implementation-specific optimization.

lessons.title: Inspecting a running page
lessons.focus: Use the Elements, Styles, Console, and Network panels to form and test a debugging hypothesis.

objectives: Use browser developer tools to locate a rendering or behavior defect.
Change one suspected cause at a time and verify it with evidence.
explanation: Debug from an observable symptom. Reproduce it, inspect the relevant element and computed styles, check the console for script errors, and check the Network panel for missing files. Then form a small hypothesis: for example, a selector does not match, a stylesheet failed to load, or an event handler never ran.

Change one cause at a time. Retest the original case and a nearby case after each fix. Developer-tool edits are temporary; record the source-file change and reload to verify the actual project, not only the inspector's in-memory override.

example.code: Profile ready
walkthrough: Symptom: the status text has no expected color.
Inspect the paragraph's computed styles and see whether a matching rule appears.
Check Network: a 404 for style.css points to the filename or path. If the file loaded, inspect selector matching and cascade instead.
Fix the root cause in the source and reload to confirm.

misconceptions: Seeing a CSS declaration in a file does not prove that the browser loaded it or that it wins the cascade.
Repeatedly changing unrelated styles makes the cause harder to isolate.

check.prompt: A rule appears in styles.css, but the element does not show its color. Name two distinct checks that separate a loading problem from a selector/cascade problem.
check.answer: Check the Network panel for a successful stylesheet request, then inspect the element's Styles/Computed panels to see whether the selector matches and whether another declaration wins.
check.explanation: Each check tests a different stage: resource loading versus rule matching and cascade.

lessons.title: Project structure and version control
lessons.focus: Name files and folders clearly, and save a working history with Git so each change can be reviewed or reverted.

objectives: Organize a small static project so each file has a clear purpose.
Use Git commits as reviewable checkpoints and avoid committing secrets.
explanation: Keep the browser entry document easy to find, use predictable file names, and group related assets in folders only when that improves navigation. Relative URLs such as ./styles.css resolve from the HTML document's location, so moving a file can break a reference even when its contents are unchanged.

Git records snapshots. Check git status to see edits, stage only the files for a coherent change, and commit with a message that says what changed. A commit makes review and rollback easier; it is not a substitute for backups or remote collaboration. Never add credentials or private keys to a repository.

example.code:
web-studio/
├── index.html
├── styles.css
└── script.js

# inspect, stage selected files, and save a checkpoint
git status
git add index.html styles.css script.js
git commit -m "Add workshop page structure"
walkthrough: index.html is the entry document and links the sibling CSS and JavaScript files.
git status reveals the current working-tree changes before staging.
git add names the intended files; git commit records a labeled snapshot.

misconceptions: A folder structure does not make code modular by itself; file boundaries should have a clear purpose.
Staging every file blindly can include generated output or secrets. Review status before committing.

check.prompt: You changed two source files and see an unfamiliar .env file in git status. What should you do before staging?
check.answer: Inspect the file and status, determine whether it contains local configuration or secrets, and exclude it (for example with .gitignore) if it should not be versioned. Stage only the intended source files.
check.explanation: Reviewing the exact staged set prevents accidental disclosure and keeps commits focused.

fundamentals.title: HTML structure and semantics
fundamentals.outcome: Write meaningful, well-formed documents with native semantics and useful page metadata.

lessons.title: Document skeleton and metadata
lessons.focus: Doctype, language, title, character encoding, viewport, and metadata that describes the document.

objectives: Identify the minimum document metadata needed for a robust HTML page.
Explain how document language and title support accessibility and browser behavior.
explanation: The doctype declaration tells the browser to use standards mode. The html element is the document root; its lang attribute identifies the primary language of the page text. In the head, declare UTF-8 early, set a useful page title, and include a viewport declaration for layouts that adapt to device width. The body contains the document's visible content.

Metadata should describe the actual page. A description can help summaries in some contexts, but browsers and search systems may choose other text. The title appears in browser tabs, history, and assistive-technology context, so make it specific and concise. Keep the language tag accurate; it helps pronunciation and language-sensitive processing.

example.code: Repair workshops
walkthrough: The doctype precedes the root element so the document uses standards mode.
lang="en" declares the page's primary language; use a suitable BCP 47 language tag for other languages or regional variants.
The encoding and viewport declarations support reliable text decoding and device-width layout.
The title names this page rather than repeating a generic site label.

misconceptions: The viewport meta element does not make a page responsive by itself; CSS must still adapt layout.
A meta description is not a guaranteed search-result snippet and should not be treated as a ranking switch.

check.prompt: A page has a useful visible heading but its browser tab says 'Untitled'. Which metadata should you add, and which element should contain the visible page heading?
check.answer: Add a descriptive <title> inside <head>; keep the visible page heading in a heading element such as <h1> inside <body>.
check.explanation: The document title and visible heading serve different contexts. One labels the page outside the content; the other structures and names its visible content.

lessons.title: Text, links, images, lists, and tables
lessons.focus: Choose elements by meaning; write descriptive links and text alternatives; use tables for tabular data.

objectives: Choose semantic elements for text, navigation, images, lists, and tabular data.
Write links and alternative text that make sense outside their visual context.
explanation: Use elements according to the meaning of the content. Headings create a navigable outline; paragraphs group prose; lists represent related items; anchors navigate to a resource or location. A link's text should describe its destination instead of relying on 'click here'.

An image's alt text depends on its purpose. Describe meaningful information conveyed by the image. Use alt="" when an image is decorative or its information is already fully provided nearby. Tables are for relationships among data, not visual page layout; include a caption where useful, header cells, and scope so relationships remain understandable.

example.code:
Upcoming sessions

  • Repair basics, Saturday at 10:00
Workshop capacity
SessionSeats
Repair basics12
walkthrough: The unordered list groups a set of available sessions.
The descriptive link text identifies its destination without needing surrounding visual cues.
The image alt describes relevant visual information; the caption gives context for the figure.
The table caption names the data, and scoped header cells associate labels with their columns and row.

misconceptions: Alt text is not a filename or a place to repeat every nearby sentence; choose it based on the image's role.
A table is not the right tool for aligning cards or page columns; use CSS layout for presentation.

check.prompt: A decorative divider image adds no information, and a page has a small table of session names and seat counts. What should the divider's alt value be, and which table cells should be headers?
check.answer: Use alt="" for the decorative divider. Mark the column labels as <th scope="col"> and, when a row label identifies a record, use <th scope="row"> for it.
check.explanation: Empty alternative text lets assistive technology skip decoration. Header relationships make tabular data easier to navigate.

lessons.title: Landmarks and content structure
lessons.focus: Use main, header, nav, article, section, aside, and footer according to their semantics.

objectives: Use landmark elements to express a page's major regions.
Distinguish a self-contained article from a thematic section and complementary content.
explanation: Landmarks provide recognizable regions for navigation. A page generally has one main element for its unique central content, a header for introductory or navigational material, nav for a major navigation group, and footer for closing or related information. Header and footer can also belong to article or section contexts, so their meaning depends on placement.

Use article for a composition that could stand on its own, such as a post or event listing. Use section to group a thematic part of a page, normally with a heading. Aside is related but complementary content. Do not add landmarks solely for styling; CSS classes can handle visual grouping without changing meaning.

example.code:
Northside Library
Events

Community events

Repair cafe

Bring a household item and work with a volunteer.

Step-free entrance available.

Contact the library team
walkthrough: The page header contains site identity and a primary navigation landmark.
Main identifies the unique central content; its h1 gives that content a title.
The repair cafe item is independently meaningful, so article is appropriate.
The accommodation note complements the event information, while footer contains closing contact information.

misconceptions: A section is not just a generic wrapper: use it for a thematic group, usually with a heading.
Adding multiple unlabeled nav elements can make landmark navigation ambiguous; label distinct navigation groups when needed.

check.prompt: A page has a standalone event card with a title, date, and description, followed by a page-wide list of all events. Which element could represent the card, and which element should contain the page's central content?
check.answer: The standalone card can be an <article>; the page-wide central content belongs in <main>.
check.explanation: Article expresses self-contained content; main identifies the page's primary content area.

lessons.title: Attributes and element relationships
lessons.focus: Understand global attributes, IDs, classes, data attributes, and valid parent-child relationships.

objectives: Use id, class, and data-* attributes for distinct purposes.
Check that attributes and child elements are valid for their HTML context.
explanation: An id identifies one element in a document and is useful for fragment links, labels, and scripts; keep it unique. A class is a reusable set of tokens for styling or selecting groups. A data-* attribute stores an application-specific string on an element; it does not create behavior automatically. Global attributes such as lang, hidden, and tabindex have broader applicability, but each still has semantics and constraints.

HTML elements have content models that define what children are allowed. For example, a button may contain phrasing content but cannot contain another interactive control. A label should be associated with its form control. Invalid nesting can be repaired differently by browsers and can confuse accessibility tools, so validate markup rather than relying on visual appearance alone.

example.code:

Workshop details
walkthrough: The label's for value matches the input's unique id, providing an explicit accessible name.
The class can be reused by other save buttons; the data-action value is a string for application code to read.
The fragment link targets a unique section id in the same document.
The section's aria-labelledby references an existing heading id to name the region.

misconceptions: A data-action attribute is only data; JavaScript must read it and implement behavior.
Adding ARIA does not repair invalid element nesting or replace native HTML semantics.

check.prompt: Two buttons need the same visual style, while a script should identify one of them as the save action. Which attributes fit these needs, and what must remain unique?
check.answer: Use a shared class for styling and a data-action attribute for the script's action value. Any id used by either button must be unique within the document.
check.explanation: Classes group elements, data attributes carry application-specific values, and ids provide unique document identifiers.

fundamentals.title: Forms and browser-native behavior
fundamentals.outcome: Build forms that communicate purpose, use native validation, and work by keyboard.

lessons.title: Labels and control types
lessons.focus: Associate labels with controls and select input types that fit the data being collected.

objectives: Associate every form control with a persistent, programmatic label.
Choose native input types and controls that match the information and expected interaction.
explanation: A label gives a control its accessible name and enlarges the clickable target when explicitly connected with for and a matching unique id. Wrapping a control in its label is another valid association. Placeholder text is a hint, not a replacement: it can disappear while typing and often has weaker contrast. Give submitted controls a name; the name becomes the key in FormData and in ordinary form submission.

Choose a control for the data and interaction. email, url, number, date, checkbox, radio, select, and textarea expose useful native behavior, but type="number" is for quantities where incrementing makes sense, not identifiers such as postal codes. Use a button with type="submit" to submit and type="button" for unrelated actions, since a button inside a form submits by default.

example.code:
<form action="/profile" method="post">
  <label for="display-name">Display name</label>
  <input id="display-name" name="displayName" autocomplete="nickname" required minlength="2">

  <label for="email">Email address</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email" required>

  <label for="bio">Short introduction</label>
  <textarea id="bio" name="bio" rows="4" maxlength="240"></textarea>
  <button type="submit">Save profile</button>
  <button type="button" id="preview">Preview</button>
</form>
walkthrough: Each label for value matches one unique control id, so clicking the label focuses its control and the accessible name is clear.
name values identify submitted data; autocomplete describes the kind of value so the browser can offer appropriate saved information.
The email input offers email-oriented semantics and native validity checks, while textarea is appropriate for free-form multi-line text.
Explicit button types keep Save profile as the submit action and Preview from submitting the form.

misconceptions: A placeholder is not a durable label and should not carry the only instruction or name for a control.
A valid-looking email input does not prove that an address exists or belongs to the person; format validation is not identity verification.
Every button inside a form submits unless its type says otherwise; choose the type explicitly.

check.prompt: A postal-code field loses its hint once the user types, and the Preview button submits the form. What should change?
check.answer: Add a persistent label associated with the field, keep any placeholder as optional supplemental guidance, and set the Preview button to type="button".
check.explanation: Labels provide a stable accessible name, while explicit button types prevent accidental submission.

lessons.title: Grouping and instructions
lessons.focus: Use fieldset, legend, help text, required state, and error messages that are programmatically related.

objectives: Group related controls with fieldset and legend and connect help text to its control.
Communicate required and invalid states in text as well as through programmatic relationships.
explanation: Use fieldset and legend for a related group of controls, especially radio buttons or checkboxes that share one question. A legend names the group; a label names each individual option. A visual heading alone does not create this relationship. Keep instructions near the relevant control and connect supplementary text with aria-describedby when the relationship needs to be exposed to assistive technology.

The required attribute participates in native constraint validation and communicates that a value is needed. Do not rely on color or an asterisk alone: explain required status in text and mark the control with required. For custom errors, set a clear message, expose it in the control description, set aria-invalid while invalid, and provide a way to find or focus the affected field. Avoid announcing the same message through several competing live regions.

example.code:
Choose a workshop session (required)

Include the country code, for example +1 555 0100.
walkthrough: The legend gives the radio group a shared question, and the labels name the individual choices.
For same-named radio controls, required on one member makes a selection in that group necessary for native validation.
The help paragraph is referenced by the input id through aria-describedby, preserving the instruction as a programmatic description.
The instruction also states an example in text instead of relying on a visual format alone.

misconceptions: A fieldset is not a generic layout box; reserve it for a logically related set of controls and give it a useful legend.
aria-describedby supplements an accessible name; it does not replace a label.
Required state and an error message are different: required describes a constraint, while an error explains why the current value is invalid.

check.prompt: A screen reader encounters two unlabeled radio buttons beneath the visual heading “Delivery”. What HTML relationships should you add?
check.answer: Wrap the related radios in a fieldset with a legend such as “Delivery method”, and give each radio its own associated label.
check.explanation: The legend names the group and each label identifies one selectable option.

lessons.title: Constraints and submission
lessons.focus: Use built-in constraints, understand submit events, and provide clear invalid, pending, and success states.

objectives: Use native constraints such as required, minlength, min, max, and type before writing custom validation.
Handle the submit event and distinguish browser validation, application validation, and server-side validation.
explanation: HTML constraints provide a first layer of validation. required checks presence, type checks supported formats, minlength and maxlength constrain text length, and numeric or date controls can use min and max. The browser normally blocks submission when a constraint fails and focuses an invalid control. These checks improve feedback but can be bypassed, so a server must validate untrusted data independently.

The submit event fires after native constraints pass. Read FormData from the form and preventDefault only when the page is intentionally handling submission in JavaScript. For custom checks, use setCustomValidity and reportValidity, clear the custom message when the value changes, and show a specific correction. If a request is pending, prevent duplicate submits and announce status; report success only after the operation actually succeeds.

walkthrough: The required email input is checked by the browser before the submit event runs.
FormData reads the successful named controls; controls without a name are omitted.
The handler prevents navigation because this example takes responsibility for handling the submission.
In a real request, show pending state, await the response, and announce success or a useful error based on the result.

misconceptions: Client-side validation is for usability, not a security boundary; validate on the server too.
The submit event is preferable to listening only for a button click because Enter-key submission and other submitters are included.
A status message should describe an outcome that occurred; do not announce success before an asynchronous request succeeds.

check.prompt: A form has required and type="email", but the application must also reject addresses from a blocked domain. Where should each check happen?
check.answer: Keep required and basic email-format constraints in HTML for immediate browser feedback, add the domain rule in application logic for user feedback, and enforce all relevant rules again on the server.
check.explanation: Native constraints help users quickly, while server validation remains authoritative because client code can be bypassed.

lessons.title: Focus and keyboard behavior
lessons.focus: Keep a logical tab order, visible focus, and predictable submission behavior.

objectives: Preserve a logical keyboard sequence and a visible focus indicator for every interactive control.
Move focus deliberately after dynamic form errors or state changes without disrupting users.
explanation: Native controls participate in the document tab order according to their position. Avoid positive tabindex values: they create a second ordering system that becomes brittle when controls are added or moved. Use DOM order that matches the visual and task sequence. Keep a visible focus indicator with :focus-visible, and do not remove the browser outline unless an equally visible replacement is present.

When custom validation finds an error, place concise text near the relevant field, set aria-invalid="true", and relate the message with aria-describedby. If submission reveals several errors, provide a summary with links to fields and consider moving focus to the summary or first invalid control. Restore or manage focus after closing dialogs and other temporary UI. Test with keyboard alone and verify that focus is never hidden behind fixed content.

example.code: Enter at least one seat.
walkthrough: Source order puts the label, field, instruction, and action in the expected reading and keyboard sequence.
The visible focus outline helps keyboard users locate the active control; offset separates it from the control edge.
The helper text is associated with the input and can be included in its accessible description.
If validation adds an error, update the description relationship and focus strategy so the user can discover and correct it.

misconceptions: A mouse-only visual check cannot establish keyboard accessibility; operate the complete form without a pointer.
Positive tabindex values do not fix poor document order and often make navigation unpredictable.
Moving focus on every keystroke or announcing redundant updates can make a form harder to use.

check.prompt: A form uses tabindex="1" and tabindex="2" to force focus order, and CSS removes every outline. What is a robust correction?
check.answer: Remove the positive tabindex values, arrange controls in the correct DOM order, and provide a clear :focus-visible indicator.
check.explanation: Natural order is stable as the form changes, and visible focus makes keyboard position perceivable.

lessons.title: Autocomplete and input assistance
lessons.focus: Use autocomplete tokens and input modes so people can fill forms faster on any device.

objectives: Use standard autocomplete tokens for common user data and choose inputmode for convenient virtual keyboards.
Keep browser assistance optional and preserve privacy, clarity, and control.
explanation: The autocomplete attribute accepts defined tokens that describe the purpose of a value, such as name, email, street-address, postal-code, and current-password. Correct tokens can help browsers and assistive technology identify fields and offer saved values. Use the token that matches the field, and group related address fields with an appropriate section when a page collects multiple addresses.

inputmode is a hint about the virtual keyboard, not validation. For example, inputmode="numeric" can request a numeric keypad for a code while the value remains text, which preserves leading zeros. Use type="tel" for telephone numbers and type="email" for email addresses. Do not disable autocomplete broadly to force users to type; turn it off only for a specific value where saved suggestions would be inappropriate.

example.code:
<label for="full-name">Full name</label>
<input id="full-name" name="name" autocomplete="name" required>

<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email" required>

<label for="postal-code">Postal code</label>
<input id="postal-code" name="postalCode" inputmode="numeric" autocomplete="postal-code">

<label for="verification-code">Verification code</label>
<input id="verification-code" name="code" inputmode="numeric" autocomplete="one-time-code">
walkthrough: Autocomplete tokens describe data purpose and can help the browser fill familiar information accurately.
The postal code remains text, so leading zeros are preserved; inputmode only suggests a convenient keyboard.
The one-time-code token can help compatible systems offer a received verification code.
Labels remain visible and meaningful whether values are entered manually or supplied by browser assistance.

misconceptions: inputmode does not validate or change the underlying value type.
Autocomplete does not guarantee a particular browser prompt; support and user settings vary.
Autocomplete tokens should describe the actual field purpose, not be selected only to influence browser behavior.

check.prompt: A one-time verification code may start with zero, and mobile users should see a numeric keypad. Which input hints preserve the value correctly?
check.answer: Use a text input with inputmode="numeric" and autocomplete="one-time-code". The keyboard hint does not remove leading zeros or validate the code.
check.explanation: Text preserves the identifier exactly; inputmode and autocomplete provide assistance without imposing numeric arithmetic semantics.

fundamentals.title: CSS foundations and visual rules
fundamentals.outcome: Predict how the cascade, values, and box model determine an element’s final appearance and size.

lessons.title: Rules, selectors, and matching
lessons.focus: Type, class, ID, attribute, pseudo-class, pseudo-element, combinator, and selector lists.

objectives: Read common selectors and predict which elements they match.
Choose selectors that express component intent without unnecessary specificity.
explanation: A CSS rule has a selector and a declaration block. Type selectors match element names, class selectors match reusable class tokens, ID selectors match an id, and attribute selectors match attributes or values. Combinators express relationships: a space selects descendants, > direct children, + the next sibling, and ~ later siblings. Lists separated by commas share declarations; each selector in the list is evaluated independently.

Pseudo-classes select a state or structural condition, such as :hover, :focus-visible, :checked, or :first-child. Pseudo-elements target generated or specialized parts such as ::before and ::marker. Prefer classes for reusable component styling and state pseudo-classes for actual state; selectors should remain understandable as markup evolves.

example.code: Lessons Practice
walkthrough: .site-nav > a matches only links that are direct children of the navigation.
The attribute selector styles the link whose current-page state is exposed in markup.
The focus-visible pseudo-class adds a keyboard focus treatment without inventing a custom tabindex state.
The adjacent-sibling selector applies spacing only when a link follows another link.

misconceptions: A descendant selector can match deeply nested elements; use > when the direct relationship matters.
A selector matching an element does not guarantee its declaration wins; the cascade still resolves competing declarations.
Pseudo-elements use double-colon notation in modern CSS and do not replace semantic content.

check.prompt: A card title should be styled only when it is a direct child of .card, and a warning should appear when .card has a descendant with class is-warning. Which selectors express those relationships?
check.answer: Use .card > .title for the direct child. Use .card:has(.is-warning) for a card containing a matching descendant, when the supported browser target includes :has().
check.explanation: The child combinator expresses direct parentage; :has() lets the subject match based on a relative descendant selector.

lessons.title: Cascade, specificity, and inheritance
lessons.focus: Resolve origin, importance, layers, specificity, source order, and inherited values.

objectives: Resolve competing declarations using cascade order, specificity, and source order.
Explain inheritance and avoid escalating specificity to patch styling conflicts.
explanation: The cascade first considers relevance, origin and importance, and cascade-layer order; specificity and scoping proximity are considered later, with source order breaking remaining ties. For ordinary declarations, later layers outrank earlier layers, while unlayered normal author declarations outrank layered normal declarations. Important declarations reverse layer priority. User-important styles can outrank author styles, which is useful for accessibility preferences.

Specificity is compared as a tuple of ID, class/attribute/pseudo-class, and type/pseudo-element counts, not as a decimal score. :where() contributes zero specificity; :is(), :not(), and :has() take specificity from their most specific argument. Inheritance applies only to properties defined as inherited (for example color); layout properties such as margin generally do not inherit. A declared, non-inherited property still participates in the cascade and may use its initial or other default value.

walkthrough: The layer order is declared once; for normal declarations, overrides comes after components and therefore wins when specificity otherwise ties.
The unlayered normal .notice rules outrank normal layered declarations in the same origin, which is why layer strategy should be consistent.
color is inherited, but the explicit color: inherit on the link asks it to use the parent color.
If an important declaration appears, layer priority reverses; investigate the cascade before adding another important rule.

misconceptions: Specificity alone does not determine the winner; origin, importance, and layer order are resolved earlier.
CSS specificity is not a base-10 number that can be added or carried between columns.
Most properties do not inherit; inheritance is a property-level behavior, not a general tree rule.

check.prompt: Two normal author declarations target the same link: a layered selector has greater specificity than an unlayered selector. Which wins, assuming both are relevant and in the same origin?
check.answer: The unlayered normal declaration wins over declarations in author cascade layers, regardless of selector specificity.
check.explanation: Layer precedence is considered before specificity. Importance changes layer ordering, so the answer depends on declarations being normal.

lessons.title: Values, units, and custom properties
lessons.focus: Use lengths, percentages, viewport and font-relative units, functions, and design tokens.

objectives: Choose units and value functions appropriate to content, context, and viewport.
Define and consume custom properties as scoped design tokens.
explanation: CSS values include keywords, numbers, dimensions, percentages, functions, and combinations. px is a CSS reference pixel, not necessarily one hardware pixel. em is relative to the computed font size of the element for most properties; rem is relative to the root element font size. Percentages take their reference from the property and layout context. Viewport units relate to the viewport; newer small, large, and dynamic variants can help account for browser chrome on mobile. Prefer content-driven sizing where possible.

Functions such as calc(), min(), max(), and clamp() combine compatible values and express bounds. Custom properties declared with --name participate in inheritance and the cascade, and are substituted with var(). Give tokens meaningful names, provide fallbacks when useful, and scope theme overrides intentionally. A custom property used in a value is generally validated at computed-value time; a bad substitution can make that declaration invalid rather than falling back to another earlier declaration.

walkthrough: The page token provides one shared maximum width and can be overridden for a theme or component subtree.
clamp() keeps spacing and type between a minimum and maximum while allowing a fluid middle value.
The article is constrained by both its available width and a readable measure.
The custom properties inherit from :root unless a nearer element overrides them.

misconceptions: A percentage does not always mean a percentage of the parent width; its reference depends on the property and containing block.
em is not universally relative to the parent font size; for font-size it is based on the parent, while many other uses relate to the element’s computed font size.
A CSS custom property is not a compile-time constant; it participates in runtime cascade and inheritance.

check.prompt: A page needs a maximum readable width and gutters that grow on wide screens but stay usable on small ones. Which CSS value tools can express those constraints without media-query breakpoints?
check.answer: Use max-width to cap the content measure and clamp() for gutters, for example padding-inline: clamp(1rem, 4vw, 2.5rem).
check.explanation: A maximum bounds the line length while clamp provides a fluid value with explicit minimum and maximum.

lessons.title: Box model and sizing
lessons.focus: Reason about content, padding, border, margin, box-sizing, overflow, and intrinsic sizing.

objectives: Calculate an element’s rendered size under content-box and border-box sizing.
Use intrinsic sizing and overflow rules to prevent clipping and unwanted horizontal scrolling.
explanation: With content-box, width and height size the content box; padding and border add to the outside dimensions. With border-box, declared width and height include content, padding, and border. Margins remain outside both models. A common project rule is box-sizing: border-box, often applied to all elements and inherited by pseudo-elements. Width, min-width, max-width, and their block-size counterparts constrain sizing, while auto and intrinsic keywords let layout respond to content.

Overflow controls what happens when content does not fit. visible allows painting outside the box; hidden clips; clip clips without creating a scroll container; auto adds scrolling when needed; scroll reserves a scrolling mechanism. Use min-width: 0 or min-height: 0 on flex and grid items when their automatic minimum size prevents shrinking. Prefer wrapping or responsive layout to clipping meaningful text.

walkthrough: The global box-sizing rule includes padding and border in the card’s declared size.
min(100%, 38rem) keeps the card within its containing block and caps its width.
min-inline-size: 0 allows a flex or grid child to shrink below its min-content width when needed.
The code sample has an explicit horizontal scroll region so long code remains available instead of being clipped.

misconceptions: Margins are not included in border-box sizing.
overflow: hidden is not a general layout fix; it can clip focus rings, content, or positioned descendants.
A long unbreakable string can impose an automatic minimum size on grid or flex children unless the layout permits shrinking or wrapping.

check.prompt: A grid card has width: 300px, 24px padding, and a 2px border under the default content-box model. What is its outer width, and how would border-box change it?
check.answer: Its outer width is 352px (300 + 48 + 4). With box-sizing: border-box, the outer width stays 300px and the content area becomes 248px.
check.explanation: Content-box adds padding and borders outside width; border-box includes them within the declared width.

lessons.title: Typography, color, backgrounds, and borders
lessons.focus: Set readable type, contrast, decoration, surfaces, and robust visual states.

objectives: Set readable type and robust color treatments with appropriate fallbacks.
Style backgrounds and borders without obscuring content or reducing contrast.
explanation: Typography affects readability and layout. Use a system or loaded font stack with a fallback, allow text to resize, choose a comfortable line-height, and constrain long-form line length. Relative font sizing supports user preferences. Text decoration and font weight should reinforce meaning without being the only cue. Measure contrast for text and meaningful graphical boundaries against their actual adjacent colors; WCAG contrast thresholds depend on text size and role.

color sets the foreground and background-color sets the element’s background; background shorthand can combine color, images, positions, sizes, and repeat behavior. A background image is decorative unless equivalent meaning is conveyed in content. Borders contribute to visual grouping but can change box size unless sizing rules account for them. Use currentColor or design tokens when a border should follow text color, and keep focus and error states distinguishable.

walkthrough: The font stack ends with a generic fallback, so text remains readable if a preferred font is unavailable.
The article measure and line-height support comfortable long-form reading without fixed-height text boxes.
The notice border uses currentColor so it tracks the foreground; color contrast still needs to be checked against the notice background.
The link has an underline treatment, preserving a non-color cue that it is interactive.

misconceptions: A visually pleasing color pair is not necessarily accessible; verify contrast in the actual rendered states.
A background image does not provide alternative text; meaningful information needs an equivalent in the document content.
Fixed pixel font sizes and fixed-height text containers can fail when users zoom or enlarge text.

check.prompt: A link is blue on a pale background and becomes identifiable only by its color. What should you change and verify?
check.answer: Add a persistent non-color cue such as an underline, preserve a visible focus state, and verify text contrast against the rendered background for normal and interactive states.
check.explanation: Color alone may not distinguish links, and contrast should be evaluated for the actual text and state.

lessons.title: Transitions, animation, and motion
lessons.focus: Animate state changes with transitions and keyframes, and respect the reduced-motion preference.

objectives: Choose transitions for state changes and keyframes for multi-step or repeating motion.
Respect reduced-motion preferences and keep motion from carrying essential information alone.
explanation: A transition interpolates a property when its computed value changes. Set the property, duration, timing function, and optionally delay; avoid transition: all because it can animate unexpected properties. Keyframes define named points in an animation timeline and can describe multi-step motion. Motion should clarify feedback, remain brief, and avoid large or repeated movement unless essential.

Some people prefer reduced motion because animation can cause discomfort or distraction. Use prefers-reduced-motion to reduce or remove nonessential movement while preserving state and meaning. Do not rely on motion alone to communicate status, and ensure controls remain operable during animation. Prefer transform and opacity for many animated effects, but profile real interactions rather than assuming every animation is free.

walkthrough: The transition names only the properties expected to change and completes quickly.
The background color communicates hover feedback even if motion is reduced.
The active transform is a small enhancement rather than the only indication that the button was activated.
The reduced-motion rule removes the entrance animation and smooth scrolling while leaving the success icon and its meaning visible.

misconceptions: A transition does not run unless a property value changes between states.
prefers-reduced-motion should remove or reduce nonessential motion, not remove information or functionality.
Transform and opacity are often efficient choices, but their performance still depends on context and should be tested.

check.prompt: A decorative card entrance animation repeats indefinitely and the only success cue is a pulsing green glow. How should the design change?
check.answer: Make the entrance brief or remove it, respect prefers-reduced-motion, and communicate success with persistent text or another non-motion cue that does not rely on color alone.
check.explanation: Motion should be optional and nonessential; state needs a clear, persistent alternative.

fundamentals.title: Layout and responsive design
fundamentals.outcome: Build resilient layouts that respond to content, viewport size, and user settings.

lessons.title: Normal flow and formatting contexts
lessons.focus: Understand block and inline flow, containing blocks, stacking, and positioning.

objectives: Explain how normal flow, block and inline formatting, and containing blocks affect element placement.
Choose positioning and formatting behavior intentionally instead of using layout hacks.
explanation: Normal flow is the browser’s default layout model. Block-level boxes participate in block flow; inline content participates in line boxes and wraps around available space. Margin collapse can occur between certain block margins in normal flow, but flex and grid layouts establish different formatting contexts. A containing block provides the reference rectangle for sizing and positioning; its source depends on the element and positioning mode.

position: relative keeps an element in normal flow while allowing offsets and creating a reference for positioned descendants. Absolute positioning removes the element from normal flow and positions it against its containing block. Fixed positioning is usually viewport-relative; sticky positioning remains in flow until a scroll threshold is reached within its scroll container. Prefer flow, flex, or grid for primary layout, reserving offsets for overlays and small adjustments.

walkthrough: The article and aside begin in normal flow, so content remains in document order and can grow naturally.
The max-width and auto inline margins center the layout without fixed positioning.
flow-root establishes a block formatting context, containing internal floats and preventing child margins from collapsing through the container.
A later responsive layout can change the relationship between article and aside with grid or flex without changing markup order.

misconceptions: Block and inline describe layout behavior, not whether an element is semantically important.
position: relative does not remove an element from normal flow; absolute and fixed positioning do.
z-index cannot repair every overlap; containing blocks and stacking contexts determine which elements can be compared.

check.prompt: A sidebar is positioned with position:absolute, overlaps long article text, and leaves an empty area where it used to be. Why does this happen, and what layout should you consider?
check.answer: Absolute positioning removes the sidebar from normal flow, so the article does not reserve space and may overlap it. Use grid or flex for the article/sidebar relationship, reserving absolute positioning for a true overlay.
check.explanation: Primary page layout should normally remain in flow so content sizing and reading order work together.

lessons.title: Flexbox
lessons.focus: Use axes, alignment, wrapping, flexible sizing, gaps, and ordering for one-dimensional layouts.

objectives: Use the main and cross axes to predict Flexbox sizing and alignment.
Choose wrapping, gaps, and flexible sizing for one-dimensional layouts.
explanation: Flexbox lays out items along one main axis and aligns them along a perpendicular cross axis. flex-direction chooses the main axis; justify-content distributes space along it, while align-items and align-self control cross-axis alignment. The axis changes when direction is row versus column and can be influenced by writing mode, so avoid treating “horizontal” and “vertical” as universal synonyms.

A flex container may wrap items with flex-wrap. gap sets spacing between items without margin edge cases. flex-grow shares positive free space, flex-shrink controls shrinking when space is constrained, and flex-basis supplies the starting main size; the flex shorthand combines these behaviors. Items have an automatic minimum size based on content in common cases, so min-width: 0 or min-height: 0 may be needed to allow shrinking. The order property changes visual order without changing source or keyboard order, so use it cautiously.

walkthrough: The toolbar’s main axis is the inline direction by default in a horizontal writing mode.
align-items centers items on the cross axis; justify-content distributes the two groups along the main axis.
Wrapping lets controls move to another line when the available width is small.
Nested actions form their own flex container, with gap defining spacing without altering source order.

misconceptions: justify-content follows the main axis, which is not always the horizontal axis.
flex: 1 can make items grow and shrink; it does not simply mean “equal width” in every context.
Visual reordering does not change screen-reader or keyboard order; keep source order meaningful.

check.prompt: A row of navigation actions should use remaining space between a logo and the actions, but wrap cleanly on a narrow screen. Which Flexbox properties help, and what must remain true of the markup?
check.answer: Use display:flex, justify-content:space-between, flex-wrap:wrap, and a gap for spacing. Keep the DOM order meaningful because wrapping and visual alignment do not change reading or keyboard order.
check.explanation: Flexbox handles one-dimensional alignment and wrapping, while accessible sequence comes from source order.

lessons.title: CSS Grid
lessons.focus: Define tracks, gaps, placement, repeat patterns, and responsive grids for two-dimensional layouts.

objectives: Define explicit and implicit grid tracks and place items using lines or named areas.
Build responsive track patterns with repeat(), minmax(), and auto-fit/auto-fill.
explanation: CSS Grid is a two-dimensional layout system with rows and columns. grid-template-columns and grid-template-rows define explicit tracks; items not placed into those tracks can create implicit tracks controlled by grid-auto-rows or grid-auto-columns. Gaps create space between tracks. Items can be positioned by line numbers, named lines, or named template areas. Grid placement changes visual arrangement, so source order should still make sense.

The fr unit distributes available space after fixed and intrinsic sizing contributions are considered. minmax() gives a track a minimum and maximum; repeat() repeats a pattern. auto-fit collapses empty repeated tracks so occupied tracks can expand, while auto-fill preserves empty track slots. For responsive cards, repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 15rem), 1fr)) can create as many columns as fit without a breakpoint. Use minmax(0, 1fr) when a track must shrink below its min-content contribution.

walkthrough: The list remains in meaningful source order while CSS arranges its items in two dimensions.
auto-fit creates the number of columns that fit the available space and expands occupied tracks.
minmax() prevents a card from becoming narrower than the chosen minimum when room permits, while min(100%, 15rem) avoids overflow in a very narrow container.
The zero minimum on each item lets long content wrap instead of forcing a grid track wider than the container.

misconceptions: 1fr does not always mean a fixed equal fraction of the container before intrinsic content is considered.
auto-fit and auto-fill differ when the grid has room for empty tracks.
Grid can change visual placement without changing source order, so do not use it to create a confusing reading sequence.

check.prompt: A two-column grid overflows because one card contains a long unbreakable value. Which track definition and item sizing adjustment can allow the column to shrink?
check.answer: Use a flexible track such as minmax(0, 1fr) and allow the item to shrink with min-width:0; also consider overflow-wrap:anywhere for the long value.
check.explanation: The min-content automatic minimum can prevent a grid track or item from shrinking unless the minimum is relaxed.

lessons.title: Responsive rules and queries
lessons.focus: Use content-driven breakpoints, media features, container queries, and reduced-motion preferences.

objectives: Choose breakpoints based on content needs and use media queries for viewport or user preferences.
Use container queries when a component’s available size matters more than the whole viewport.
explanation: Responsive design adapts to available space, input capability, and user preferences. Start with a layout that works for the narrowest realistic content, then add breakpoints when the content needs more room; avoid targeting named devices. Media queries can test viewport dimensions, orientation, hover and pointer capabilities, color scheme, and reduced-motion preference. A breakpoint should change a layout only when the current arrangement stops working.

Container queries let a component respond to its own container size rather than the viewport. Establish an inline-size query container with container-type: inline-size, then use @container with a condition and optionally a container name. Container queries work well for reusable cards and tool panels embedded in different layouts. They do not replace flexible intrinsic sizing; combine them with wrapping, minmax(), and max-width for resilience between thresholds.

Below 42rem of container inline size, the workspace stays in one column and its content can wrap naturally.
Once the container has enough room, the layout places main material and supporting content in two columns with shrinkable tracks.
The media query responds to a user preference independently of the component’s container width.

misconceptions: A container query tests the size of an ancestor query container, not the queried element’s own final width.
A viewport media query may be the wrong tool for a reusable component that appears in multiple sized regions.
Breakpoints should follow content pressure and be tested around the threshold, not selected from a device list.

check.prompt: A reusable lesson card appears in a wide page column and a narrow sidebar. It should become two columns only when its own space permits. Should you use a viewport media query or container query, and why?
check.answer: Use a container query on an ancestor that establishes an inline-size query container, because the card’s local available width differs from the viewport width.
check.explanation: Container queries make component layout respond to its embedding context.

lessons.title: Images and intrinsic content
lessons.focus: Use responsive image sources, object fitting, and min/max sizing for long or variable content.

objectives: Choose responsive image sources and sizes appropriate to the rendered slot and pixel density.
Prevent intrinsic media and long content from forcing page overflow.
explanation: Images have intrinsic dimensions and aspect ratios. Set max-inline-size:100% and block-size:auto for fluid images that preserve ratio, or give a predictable aspect-ratio and use object-fit when cropping is intentional. The img element’s width and height attributes communicate intrinsic dimensions and help reserve layout space before loading. Use srcset with width descriptors and a sizes value that describes the rendered slot so the browser can choose an appropriate resource; use picture when art direction or format selection is needed.

Content can impose minimum sizes: long words, code, tables, and media may exceed their container. Apply overflow-wrap:anywhere to arbitrary text when breaking is acceptable; place wide code or data tables in a labeled horizontal scroll region when preserving line structure matters. For flex and grid children, set min-width:0 where their automatic minimum blocks shrinking. Do not indiscriminately hide overflow, because it can make content unreachable.

walkthrough: Width descriptors identify each source’s intrinsic pixel width; sizes estimates the image’s CSS slot so the browser can select a resource.
The width and height attributes reserve the intrinsic ratio during loading, reducing layout shift.
The alt text conveys the informative image’s content; a decorative image would instead use alt="".
The CSS caps the rendered image at its container and preserves ratio. object-fit:cover crops only if the box ratio differs from the source.

misconceptions: srcset alone with width descriptors does not describe the rendered slot; sizes supplies that estimate.
object-fit changes how replaced content fills its box; it does not make the box responsive by itself.
overflow:hidden can conceal meaningful content and keyboard focus; choose wrapping or a deliberate scroll region instead.

check.prompt: A responsive article image shifts the page while loading and appears pixelated on high-density screens. What markup information and source-selection attributes address these problems?
check.answer: Provide accurate width and height attributes to reserve the image’s intrinsic ratio, then provide srcset candidates and a sizes value that describes its rendered CSS slot.
check.explanation: Dimensions stabilize layout, and responsive source selection lets the browser choose a suitable resource for slot size and density.

lessons.title: Positioning and stacking
lessons.focus: Use position values, z-index, and stacking contexts to layer overlays, badges, and menus without surprises.

objectives: Distinguish relative, absolute, fixed, and sticky positioning and identify their containing blocks.
Explain stacking contexts and use z-index within an intentional layering system.
explanation: Relative positioning offsets an element from its normal position without removing its original space. Absolute positioning removes it from normal flow and positions it against its containing block, often established by a positioned ancestor. Fixed positioning is usually viewport-relative, though transforms and related properties on ancestors can establish a containing block. Sticky positioning participates in flow and sticks within a scroll container after its inset threshold is reached; it needs a non-auto inset on the relevant axis and room to move.

z-index orders positioned elements and certain flex/grid items, but values are compared within stacking contexts. Properties such as transform, opacity below 1, isolation:isolate, and some containment or positioned z-index cases can create a stacking context. A child with z-index:9999 cannot escape a lower parent stacking context to cover an element in a higher one. Define a small layer scale and inspect ancestor contexts when an overlay appears behind something unexpectedly.

Logical inset properties place the badge relative to writing direction and block flow.
isolation:isolate creates a local stacking context, so the badge’s z-index is compared inside that card context.
A dialog backdrop needs a deliberate application-level layer token; a large child z-index alone cannot escape an ancestor stacking context.

misconceptions: position:sticky is constrained by its scroll container and containing block; it is not always attached to the viewport.
A high z-index number does not globally outrank every other element because stacking contexts are nested.
Absolute positioning is appropriate for overlays and badges, but using it for main content layout removes content from normal flow.

check.prompt: A tooltip has z-index:9999 but still appears behind a sibling panel. The tooltip lives inside a transformed card. What should you inspect and change?
check.answer: Inspect the stacking contexts of the tooltip’s ancestors and the sibling panel. The transform creates a stacking context that contains the tooltip; adjust the parent-level layer order or move the overlay to an appropriate shared overlay root.
check.explanation: A child’s z-index is compared only within its stacking context, so increasing its number cannot cross the ancestor context boundary.

fundamentals.title: Reusable CSS and styling systems
fundamentals.outcome: Organize styles for reuse and compare native CSS with common styling tools.

lessons.title: Custom properties and design tokens
lessons.focus: Create scoped tokens, theme variants, and meaningful fallbacks.

objectives: Define CSS custom properties as reusable design tokens and explain their cascade and inheritance.
Provide intentional fallbacks and scope token changes to components or themes.
explanation: A custom property uses a name beginning with two hyphens and is consumed with var(). Unlike a preprocessor variable, it remains in the stylesheet at runtime, inherits by default, and participates in the cascade. This lets a theme or component subtree override a value without generating a separate selector for every component. Use tokens for decisions that recur, such as spacing, colors, radii, and typography, and name them for their role rather than their current literal value.

The second argument to var() is a fallback used when the custom property is missing or invalid at substitution time. It does not generally recover from a value that exists but is invalid for the consuming property. The @property rule can declare a syntax, initial value, and inheritance behavior for a custom property where supported. Keep token scopes understandable: global foundation tokens can feed semantic aliases, which then feed component styles.

walkthrough: Root properties provide defaults inherited by descendants.
The data-theme selector changes only the dark surface and text tokens, so the brand token remains shared.
A component-specific token can override a semantic theme token, with a final literal fallback for missing values.
The feature query applies color-mix only when the browser supports the syntax.

misconceptions: Custom properties are runtime values and can vary by element; they are not simple text-replacement constants.
The var() fallback is used for a missing or invalid custom property, not every invalid computed declaration that consumes it.
Tokens do not guarantee accessible color combinations; test each foreground and surface pairing in every theme.

check.prompt: A component reads var(--panel-gap, 1rem), but an ancestor defines --panel-gap: nonsense. Will the consuming declaration reliably use 1rem as its fallback?
check.answer: No. Because --panel-gap is defined, the var() fallback is not a general fallback for a value that is invalid for the consuming property; that declaration may become invalid at computed-value time. Fix the token at its source or validate it with an appropriate @property registration.
check.explanation: The fallback argument handles a missing or invalid custom property value during substitution, not all invalid values in the final property context.

lessons.title: Architecture and component styling
lessons.focus: Name classes, control scope, reduce accidental coupling, and organize responsive states.

objectives: Choose class names and component boundaries that communicate purpose and limit style leakage.
Organize CSS around predictable layers, responsive states, and reusable variants.
explanation: Component CSS should make its intended scope easy to see. A naming convention such as block__element--modifier can communicate the component relationship without requiring a framework. Use classes for reusable styling, keep selectors shallow, and prefer a component root or explicit variant class over selectors that depend on deep markup. Avoid styling based on incidental DOM structure when the structure may change.

A maintainable stylesheet has an order that readers can predict: reset or base rules, tokens, layout, components, utilities, and narrowly scoped overrides. Cascade layers can make these priorities explicit. Put responsive rules near the component they change or organize them consistently, and keep state styles such as hover, focus-visible, disabled, and invalid complete. Reuse a component when its behavior and meaning repeat; do not abstract one-off differences into an unbounded set of modifiers.

walkthrough: The layer declaration establishes a predictable priority order for normal declarations.
The notice component owns its root, title, body, and warning variant styles.
The modifier changes one local token, allowing the base component rule to remain shared.
The media query stays with the component rule whose spacing it changes.

misconceptions: A naming convention helps humans understand scope but does not create CSS encapsulation by itself.
More selectors and modifiers do not automatically mean better reuse; abstractions should reflect repeated intent.
Cascade layers affect precedence; they do not prevent selectors from matching elements outside a component.

check.prompt: A card style depends on main > section:nth-child(2) .card h2 and breaks when an introductory section is added. How would you make the styling more resilient?
check.answer: Give the relevant component and heading explicit classes, such as .lesson-card and .lesson-card__title, and keep selectors scoped to those names. Use a variant class or token for meaningful differences.
check.explanation: Purposeful class hooks reduce coupling to incidental document position and nesting.

lessons.title: Sass and SCSS
lessons.focus: Variables, nesting, mixins, functions, modules, loops, and the CSS they compile to.

objectives: Distinguish Sass variables from runtime CSS custom properties and use module-oriented Sass syntax.
Use nesting, mixins, functions, extension, and control directives without obscuring generated CSS.
explanation: Sass is a stylesheet preprocessor with SCSS syntax that is mostly CSS-compatible. Sass variables such as $space are resolved at compile time; CSS custom properties remain dynamic in the browser. Modern Sass uses @use to load modules with namespaces and @forward to expose a deliberate public API. Partials conventionally begin with an underscore and are imported through modules without the underscore or extension. Prefer modules over the legacy global @import mechanism.

Nesting groups related selectors, but deep nesting can create high-specificity selectors and tightly couple styles to markup; keep nesting shallow. Mixins emit reusable declaration or rule blocks and can accept arguments. Functions return values. @extend shares selector rules and can unexpectedly group selectors, so use it sparingly; a mixin or shared class is often clearer. @if, @for, @each, and @while generate conditional or repeated output at build time. Inspect compiled CSS: abstraction is useful only when the result remains predictable and reasonably small. A Sass function can perform a calculation and return a value; @each iterates a map or list to generate related rules. @for is useful for a bounded numeric range, @while repeats until a condition changes, and @if selects output at compile time. Use these directives only when they reduce repetition without hiding the resulting CSS.

walkthrough: The Sass variable and map are compile-time values; CSS custom properties would remain available for runtime theme changes.
@use loads Sass modules with namespaces, while sass:math supplies unit-aware division for the px-to-rem function.
The mixin emits its focus declarations at the include site, and the nested selector compiles to .button:focus-visible.
The @each loop generates two predictable utility rules; the simplified compiled CSS makes the emitted selectors and values visible.

misconceptions: Sass variables and CSS custom properties have different lifecycles: Sass values disappear during compilation, while custom properties remain dynamic.
Nesting is not free encapsulation; deeply nested rules compile into long selectors.
@extend does not simply copy declarations and may create grouped selectors with surprising reach; inspect its output.

check.prompt: A color must change when a user switches themes without recompiling the stylesheet. Should it be stored only in a Sass variable or in a CSS custom property, and why?
check.answer: Use a CSS custom property for the runtime theme value. Sass variables are resolved during compilation and cannot respond to a browser-side theme change on their own.
check.explanation: Choose the value mechanism according to when it needs to change: build time for Sass, runtime cascade for CSS custom properties.

lessons.title: Utility and component frameworks
lessons.focus: Compare Bootstrap, Bulma, and Tailwind patterns, configuration, and generated styles.

objectives: Compare utility classes, component classes, and framework-generated styles by their tradeoffs.
Customize a framework through its intended configuration or token mechanisms rather than scattered overrides.
explanation: Utility-first styling composes small classes in markup; it keeps a component’s visual recipe close to the element but can make markup dense. Component frameworks provide named components and conventions that accelerate common UI patterns, while often requiring customization for a distinct design system. Semantic component CSS uses project-owned classes and tokens, giving explicit control at the cost of authoring more styles. None of these choices guarantees accessibility; the resulting HTML semantics, keyboard behavior, contrast, and responsive states still need review.

Framework customization should use its supported theme system. Some frameworks generate utilities from configuration or Sass maps at build time, while runtime CSS custom properties can vary themes without rebuilding. Avoid layering large amounts of overrides on top of framework defaults: it increases cascade complexity and makes upgrades harder. Pick one clear source of truth for each design decision, document the chosen convention, and inspect the compiled CSS for unused or conflicting output.

example.code: Start practice Start practice
walkthrough: The utility example composes many small classes directly on the link; the class vocabulary must exist in the selected utility system.
The component example places the same intent behind one project-owned class.
A framework can supply either utilities or components, but its configuration and build process determine which classes and tokens are available.
Both links remain anchors because they navigate; styling does not determine semantic element choice.

misconceptions: Utility-first does not mean “no design system”; consistent tokens and conventions still matter.
A framework class name cannot be assumed to exist unless the framework and its build configuration generate it.
Adding ARIA or framework components does not automatically make an interaction accessible.

check.prompt: A team has 40 repeated framework overrides for colors, spacing, and radii. What should it investigate before adding more overrides?
check.answer: Identify the framework’s supported configuration, theme tokens, Sass variables/maps, and CSS custom properties. Move repeated decisions to that supported source of truth and remove redundant overrides deliberately.
check.explanation: Using the framework’s intended customization mechanism reduces conflicting cascade layers and upgrade friction.

lessons.title: Theming and color schemes
lessons.focus: Build light and dark palettes from the same tokens, and follow the user's prefers-color-scheme setting.

objectives: Build light and dark theme values with semantic tokens and a clear precedence policy.
Respect system color-scheme preferences while allowing an explicit user-selected theme.
explanation: A theme should express semantic roles such as canvas, surface, text, muted text, border, and action rather than “light blue” or “dark gray.” Assign a complete palette to each theme so a component does not have to guess how to invert individual colors. Check text and non-text contrast in every state, including focus, disabled, error, and selected states. Color should not be the only way to communicate a distinction.

prefers-color-scheme reports the user’s system preference. It can provide a default, while an explicit user choice should take precedence and persist according to the product’s policy. Avoid a first-paint flash by applying the chosen theme before rendering when practical. The color-scheme property can tell browser-provided controls which scheme they should use. Theme switches should update tokens without changing content or focus, and should be testable with system preferences and manual overrides.

walkthrough: Root tokens define the light palette and a role for each color.
The dark media query applies when the system requests dark mode unless the user explicitly selected light.
An explicit dark choice applies regardless of the system setting, and color-scheme updates native controls.
The same component styles consume semantic tokens in either mode, but each pairing still needs contrast verification.

misconceptions: prefers-color-scheme is a preference signal, not a substitute for a user-facing theme choice when the product offers one.
A dark theme is not made accessible by mechanically inverting every color.
The CSS color-scheme property influences browser-rendered controls; it does not theme all application components automatically.

check.prompt: The operating system requests dark mode, but a user has explicitly selected light mode in the app. Which should win, and how should the CSS express that policy?
check.answer: The explicit user selection should win. Apply system dark tokens only when no explicit light choice is present, such as with :root:not([data-theme="light"]) inside the preference query, and give the explicit theme selector its own token set.
check.explanation: A clear precedence policy prevents system preference from overriding a deliberate in-app choice.
